title: Trump says AI data centres should pay 'dividends' in pre-midterm shift
content:
Trump says AI data centres should pay ‘dividends’ in pre-midterm shift
US president has continued to support data centres in advance of midterms, despite growing opposition from Republicans.
United States President Donald Trump has said AI data centres should pay “dividends” to communities, in a shift before the midterm elections.
“If companies want to make their Data Centers popular, pay the community, and/or individuals within the community, a ‘dividend'” Trump said in a post on Truth Social on Wednesday.
The president’s comments come after he doubled down on his support for data centres, a stance seen as one of several political liabilities for Republicans in the run-up to the midterm election, as Trump’s approval rating has hit record lows.
Polls show dismal support for such centres amid concerns about the sprawling complexes’ water and energy use.
In the post, Trump advised companies that they could make the centres popular if they “pay the community, and/or individuals within the community, a ‘dividend’.”
“I have watched the process closely, and Data Centers that were highly unpopular in a certain area, have become extremely popular when a financial deal is struck,” he said. “MAKE DEALS, and get them built!!!”
Several top Republican candidates have opposed data centres before the midterm polls, with the issue emerging as an area of rare bipartisan consensus in advance of the November 3 vote.
Republican Senate candidates, including Ken Paxton in Texas, Mike Rogers in Michigan and John Husted in Ohio, have all called for more restrictions and oversight on the centres, in a reversal of earlier positions.
The issue featured prominently in a recent debate in Iowa, where Republican Senate Candidate Ashley Hinson said the local level should decide whether to build AI data centres.
Despite the shifting sentiment, Trump in late August issued an impassioned defence of data centres, decrying what he called “the anti-Data Center movement” as a gift to China.
“The only reason that communities throughout the USA should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” Trump wrote at the time.
“If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign.”
Trump has taken several measures to accelerate data centre development, including issuing an executive order last year that called for measures to fast-track permitting and environmental review. The order promised to use federal land for the “expeditious and orderly development of data centers”.
Trump has also backed a voluntary pledge by AI companies to cover the full cost of the electricity data centres use, but has avoided supporting legally binding federal restrictions.
A Gallup poll conducted in March suggested that 71 percent of Americans opposed establishing AI data centres in their areas.
An ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll released on Wednesday identified a similar rate of disapproval, with 72 percent of respondents saying that they opposed building new data centres in their communities.

report.summary: Trump urged AI data centre operators to pay communities a 'dividend', softening his stance as bipartisan opposition to data centres grows ahead of the November 3 midterms.
report.background: AI data centres have become an unexpected political flashpoint in the United States. The buildout driven by hyperscalers — Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta and OpenAI's partners — has expanded rapidly, and with it concerns over electricity demand, water consumption for cooling, land use and local rate increases. Trump had previously championed the industry aggressively, issuing an executive order to fast-track permitting and environmental review and opening federal land to development, framing opposition as a gift to China. He also backed a voluntary corporate pledge to cover data centres' electricity costs. But polling shows roughly seven in ten Americans oppose new data centres in their communities, and Republican Senate candidates in Texas, Michigan, Ohio and Iowa have broken with the president to demand restrictions. With his approval ratings at record lows before the midterms, Trump is repositioning rather than reversing — endorsing voluntary community payments instead of binding federal rules.
key_points: Trump posted on Truth Social that data centre companies should pay a 'dividend' to host communities or individuals, arguing that facilities which were 'highly unpopular' become 'extremely popular when a financial deal is struck'. The advice is voluntary, not a legal requirement.

The shift follows months of unwavering support. In August Trump attacked the 'anti-Data Center movement' as a gift to China, warning that communities rejecting facilities would end up 'backwards and poor'.

Opposition is now bipartisan. Republican Senate candidates Ken Paxton (Texas), Mike Rogers (Michigan), John Husted (Ohio) and Ashley Hinson (Iowa) have all called for more oversight or local control — a reversal of earlier positions.

Polling is stark: a March Gallup survey found 71 percent of Americans opposed local data centres, and an ABC/Washington Post/Ipsos poll released the same week put disapproval at 72 percent, driven by water and energy concerns.

Concrete policy remains limited. Trump has fast-tracked permits and federal land use by executive order and endorsed a voluntary pledge by AI firms to cover electricity costs, but has avoided legally binding federal restrictions.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the signal is that social licence is becoming as important as compute. Companies may need to budget for community benefit payments, local tax deals and grid upgrades as a cost of doing business, particularly in water-stressed or politically competitive regions. Developers building or siting infrastructure should expect longer negotiations, more disclosure demands and local referenda risks. For regular users, the practical stakes are electricity bills and water supplies — costs that could be passed through as higher cloud and API pricing, or mitigated if community deals and voluntary power-cost pledges hold. Watch for voluntary 'dividends' becoming a de facto standard that states then codify into binding rules.
report.tools: Track the debate with Electricity Maps (real-time grid carbon and demand), the IEA's Energy and AI data portal, Data Center Map and DataCenterHawk for facility locations, and WattTime for marginal emissions. Open-source options include Cloud Carbon Footprint and the Green Software Foundation's SCI specification for measuring workload emissions. For local advocacy, municipal permit filings and state public utility commission dockets are the most reliable primary sources.
